questions.stem: In this diagram of the vagus and phrenic nerves in the thorax, the left recurrent laryngeal nerve is shown hooking around a specific structure before ascending back to the larynx. This anatomical relationship explains why left recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy (hoarseness) can result from which of the following?

choices.label: C
choices.text: A thyroid nodule at the level of the cricoid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Compression of the phrenic nerve at the diaphragm

choices.label: E
choices.text: An aortic arch aneurysm or mass at the aortopulmonary window

explanation.summary: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the arch of the aorta at the ligamentum arteriosum, so pathology at the aortic arch or aortopulmonary window can stretch or compress it, producing hoarseness (Ortner syndrome).
explanation.whyCorrect: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the arch of the aorta at the ligamentum arteriosum, so pathology at the aortic arch or aortopulmonary window can stretch or compress it, producing hoarseness (Ortner syndrome).

questions.stem: This posterior mediastinal dissection shows a muscular tube descending behind the heart, crossed by a nerve plexus and passing through the diaphragm. Which structure is the central tubular organ shown running from the neck to the abdomen?

explanation.summary: The figure traces the esophagus from its cervical part through the thorax (surrounded by the esophageal plexus formed by the vagus nerves) to its abdominal part after passing through the diaphragmatic hiatus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The figure traces the esophagus from its cervical part through the thorax (surrounded by the esophageal plexus formed by the vagus nerves) to its abdominal part after passing through the diaphragmatic hiatus.

questions.stem: This cadaveric dissection of an opened thorax with the lungs removed exposes the central compartment between the two pleural cavities. What region of the body is displayed?

explanation.summary: With the ribs spread and lungs removed, the dissection reveals the mediastinum, the central thoracic compartment containing the great vessels, trachea, esophagus, and heart, bounded laterally by the pleural sacs.
explanation.whyCorrect: With the ribs spread and lungs removed, the dissection reveals the mediastinum, the central thoracic compartment containing the great vessels, trachea, esophagus, and heart, bounded laterally by the pleural sacs.

questions.stem: This illustration highlights a nerve looping beneath a fibrous remnant near the aortic arch. What embryologic vessel does the ligamentum arteriosum represent, and what is its clinical relevance to the adjacent nerve?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus, and the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under it

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the remnant of the foramen ovale draining into the atrium

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a persistent left superior vena cava that compresses the phrenic nerve

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is the obliterated ductus venosus supplying the esophagus

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the remnant of the umbilical vein and unrelated to any nerve

explanation.summary: The ligamentum arteriosum is the postnatal remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus; the left recurrent laryngeal nerve passes under the arch just lateral to it, so an aortic aneurysm or mass here can entrap the nerve and cause hoarseness.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ligamentum arteriosum is the postnatal remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus; the left recurrent laryngeal nerve passes under the arch just lateral to it, so an aortic aneurysm or mass here can entrap the nerve and cause hoarseness.

questions.stem: In this anterior view of the opened thorax, a lobulated glandular structure sits in the superior/anterior mediastinum just deep to the manubrium, overlying the great vessels and pericardium. In an adult this organ is typically atrophied, but what is it?

explanation.summary: The thymus lies in the anterior mediastinum behind the manubrium; prominent in children, it involutes with age. Its location makes it a common source of anterior mediastinal masses (e.g., thymoma).
explanation.whyCorrect: The thymus lies in the anterior mediastinum behind the manubrium; prominent in children, it involutes with age. Its location makes it a common source of anterior mediastinal masses (e.g., thymoma).

questions.stem: This diagram traces a lymphatic channel that ascends through the posterior mediastinum from an abdominal dilation to empty at the junction of two veins on the left side of the neck. Where does this channel drain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Into the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Directly into the superior vena cava

choices.label: E
choices.text: Into the junction of the right internal jugular and right subclavian veins

explanation.summary: The thoracic duct begins at the cisterna chyli, ascends through the posterior mediastinum, and empties into the venous system at the left jugulosubclavian (venous) angle, returning lymph and chyle from most of the body.
explanation.whyCorrect: The thoracic duct begins at the cisterna chyli, ascends through the posterior mediastinum, and empties into the venous system at the left jugulosubclavian (venous) angle, returning lymph and chyle from most of the body.

questions.stem: This diagram maps numerous named nodal groups (paratracheal, tracheobronchial, juxtaesophageal, juxtavertebral, diaphragmatic, and others) distributed through the thorax. What functional network does it depict?

choices.label: B
choices.text: The lymphatic drainage of the mediastinum

choices.label: C
choices.text: The distribution of the vagus nerve branches

choices.label: E
choices.text: The sympathetic ganglia of the thoracic chain

explanation.summary: The figure illustrates the mediastinal lymph node stations; knowledge of these groups underlies cancer staging, as tumor spread to specific nodal stations determines resectability and prognosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The figure illustrates the mediastinal lymph node stations; knowledge of these groups underlies cancer staging, as tumor spread to specific nodal stations determines resectability and prognosis.

questions.stem: This lateral schematic divides the mediastinum into compartments using a horizontal plane. The dashed line separating the superior mediastinum from the inferior compartments passes through which surface landmark?

explanation.summary: The transverse thoracic plane runs from the sternal angle (angle of Louis) posteriorly to the T4/T5 disc, dividing the mediastinum into superior and inferior parts; the inferior is further split into anterior, middle, and posterior compartments.
explanation.whyCorrect: The transverse thoracic plane runs from the sternal angle (angle of Louis) posteriorly to the T4/T5 disc, dividing the mediastinum into superior and inferior parts; the inferior is further split into anterior, middle, and posterior compartments.

questions.stem: In this lateral cadaveric view of the inferior mediastinum, the dashed outline lies between the sternum in front and the pericardium/heart behind. Which mediastinal compartment contains mainly the heart and roots of the great vessels?

explanation.summary: The inferior mediastinum is subdivided into anterior (sternum to pericardium), middle (the pericardium and its contents, i.e., heart and great vessel roots), and posterior (behind the pericardium, containing esophagus and descending aorta).
explanation.whyCorrect: The inferior mediastinum is subdivided into anterior (sternum to pericardium), middle (the pericardium and its contents, i.e., heart and great vessel roots), and posterior (behind the pericardium, containing esophagus and descending aorta).

questions.stem: This diagram overlays the great vessels on the lungs with a horizontal reference line. The arch of the aorta both begins and ends at the level marked by this line. What vertebral/surface landmark does this line correspond to?

explanation.summary: The plane of the sternal angle (transverse thoracic plane, T4/T5) marks the beginning and end of the aortic arch, the bifurcation of the trachea, and the boundary between superior and inferior mediastinum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The plane of the sternal angle (transverse thoracic plane, T4/T5) marks the beginning and end of the aortic arch, the bifurcation of the trachea, and the boundary between superior and inferior mediastinum.

questions.stem: In a patient with a mediastinal mass obstructing the vessel labeled at the upper right of this venous diagram (the superior vena cava), which vein provides the most important collateral route returning blood to the heart?

explanation.summary: The azygos system connects the SVC and IVC territories along the posterior thoracic wall. In SVC obstruction it becomes the key collateral channel, allowing upper-body venous blood to bypass the block and reach the right atrium.
explanation.whyCorrect: The azygos system connects the SVC and IVC territories along the posterior thoracic wall. In SVC obstruction it becomes the key collateral channel, allowing upper-body venous blood to bypass the block and reach the right atrium.

questions.stem: This cadaveric dissection of the superior mediastinum shows the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. Around which structure does this nerve loop before ascending to the larynx?

explanation.summary: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch just lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum. Its long thoracic course explains hoarseness from aortic aneurysm, left atrial enlargement, or mediastinal tumor (Ortner syndrome).
explanation.whyCorrect: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch just lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum. Its long thoracic course explains hoarseness from aortic aneurysm, left atrial enlargement, or mediastinal tumor (Ortner syndrome).

questions.stem: These frontal and lateral chest radiographs plus a sagittal CT all point to an opacity located just behind the sternum. In which mediastinal compartment is this lesion located?

explanation.summary: A retrosternal mass filling the space in front of the pericardium and great vessels localizes to the anterior mediastinum, the classic site for the 'terrible Ts' (thymoma, teratoma, thyroid, lymphoma).
explanation.whyCorrect: A retrosternal mass filling the space in front of the pericardium and great vessels localizes to the anterior mediastinum, the classic site for the 'terrible Ts' (thymoma, teratoma, thyroid, lymphoma).

questions.stem: This patient shows facial fullness/plethora and prominent dilated superficial veins over the upper chest wall. This appearance is the classic presentation of which condition?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Right heart failure with peripheral edema

explanation.summary: Obstruction of the SVC (commonly by a mediastinal tumor such as lung cancer or lymphoma) impairs venous return from the head, neck, and upper chest, producing facial plethora/edema and engorged collateral chest wall veins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Obstruction of the SVC (commonly by a mediastinal tumor such as lung cancer or lymphoma) impairs venous return from the head, neck, and upper chest, producing facial plethora/edema and engorged collateral chest wall veins.

questions.stem: This coronal CT shows a lung cancer with soft tissue encircling a large thin-walled venous structure to the right of the ascending aorta. Obstruction of the encased vessel would most directly cause which clinical syndrome?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aortic dissection with limb pulse deficits

explanation.summary: The tumor wraps around the superior vena cava; malignant compression or invasion of the SVC obstructs venous return from the head, neck, and arms, producing SVC syndrome. Lung cancer is the most common cause.
explanation.whyCorrect: The tumor wraps around the superior vena cava; malignant compression or invasion of the SVC obstructs venous return from the head, neck, and arms, producing SVC syndrome. Lung cancer is the most common cause.
